The difference between an engineering team getting 2x leverage from AI and one getting 100x isn't the model—they’re running the exact same LLM weights.

As Y Combinator President Garry Tan expressed at AI Engineer, the leverage is entirely in how you wire the work.

Most enterprises treat AI agents as isolated, autocomplete chatbots. Every session starts from scratch. Every prompt is a one-off effort. The result is an organization that wakes up every single morning with operational amnesia.

Scaling an AI-native organization requires moving from prompt engineering to context architecture:

Treating AI as a Workforce, Not Autocomplete: When you deploy tools like Cursor or Claude Code, you are not writing software. You are hiring, onboarding, and directing an operational workforce defined in markdown skill files.

The Discipline of "Skillifying" Work: Doing one-off manual tasks is organizational waste. High-leverage teams refine every resolved bug, architectural decision, and review policy into a version-controlled, reusable skill file that agents can execute autonomously.

Context Engineering & The Librarian: Having an LLM isn't enough; you need a system librarian. If agents lack access to the right enterprise schemas, API contracts, and domain constraints at runtime, they hallucinate.

Abundance is not an executive slide deck. It is shipped, production-grade software.
Is your engineering organization treating AI as an interactive chat box, or architecting a persistent company brain?

What is not in the headlines yet, is the missing AI Governance piece of the puzzle.  

Anyone ask, “AI Decision ownership framework – does it exist?”

Depending on a number of factors: 
(here’s a few considerations)

1. Starting with your current role/level, suggest caution “live wire” topic.
2. Your Dept or Company’s AI stance or use, do you foresee greater risk exposure?
3. the current level of AIG in-motion, light or heavy use – low risk vs high risk?
4. Actual dangerous/catastrophic events, aware of ‘close calls’ or issues.
5. Risk level and/or category involved, in high-risk sectors: health, finance, gov’t. 

The A to I: How to approach AIG?

A. Avoid the “accusatory” or “righteous” position, focus on AIG remediation tactics.
B. Don’t go down the “scare mongering” path, it won’t inflate awareness & only deflate you.
C. Be very specific (think Use case level) where you are addressing a “solvable” AIG concern.
D. Best practices don’t exist yet, but do borrow proven steps from other disciplines (NIST).
E. Take an AIG Class, informal “brown-bag” discussions, share the wealth of AIG knowledge.
F. “AIG is a Team Sport” with End-to-End, full life-cycles, far reaching impacts.
G. Human intervention is only so good, along with Ownership, automation and design rule.
H. Skip self-inflicted wounds by incorporating safe and responsible access/boundary specs.
I.   We started with “A” and end on “I” suggests intelligent approaches start with AIG.

Four years ago we taught machines to speak human.

Turns out that was the wrong language for most of the work.

Last week TypeSafe AI released Jev. The founder, Diogo Almeida, helped build RLHF and InstructGPT at OpenAI. And the model he built after leaving can't write a single sentence.

You can't chat with it, and it won't draft your emails or your code.

You hand it a support ticket, a log line or a JSON blob, plus a list of questions with fixed answer options. It hands back a decision and how confident it is in that decision. That's the whole product.

Here's why developers are losing their minds over it:

→ Speed: 70 to 500 milliseconds per call. TypeSafe claims up to 200x faster than frontier LLMs.
→ Cost: $0.042 per million input tokens. Output is free.
→ Reliability: You define the valid answers upfront, so it can't invent one. No broken JSON, no parser, no retry loop.

Now the part people won't like.

Most AI agents in production today are over-engineered.

Open up any "agentic" workflow and count the steps. Route this ticket. Tag this document. Pick which tool to call. Check if this input is a jailbreak. Score this lead.

Every one of those is a yes, a no, or a pick from a list. And we've been running all of them through a frontier LLM, paying for paragraphs nobody reads, then writing extra code to clean up the output.

That's hiring a PhD to sort the mail.

The teams that win the next two years of AI won't have the biggest model contract. They'll be the ones who audited their agents and realised how much of the workload never needed language at all.

On TypeSafe's own benchmark, Jev sits around mid-tier LLM accuracy, below the frontier. And "can't hallucinate" means it can't return an invalid answer. It can still pick the wrong one.

But the direction is the story. LLMs think slowly and talk. Jev decides fast and stays quiet. Real systems will need both.

The companies spending the most on AI right now might be the ones using it least efficiently.

What you may work on

Work varies by workstream and may include:

Grading criteria development — taking a clinical question and breaking the ideal answer into discrete, checkable criteria, so a model response can be graded consistently rather than impressionistically.

Clinical dialogue evaluation — reviewing multi-turn clinical conversations and judging them for accuracy, safety, completeness, appropriate hedging, and whether escalation advice was correct.

Clinical reasoning annotation — recording how you would work through a case, including the differential you considered and rejected, not only the conclusion.

Output review — flagging hallucinated findings, dangerous omissions, unsupported certainty, and advice that is technically correct but clinically unsafe.

Guideline authoring — defining edge cases and standards of care for your specialty so annotation stays consistent across a large group of clinicians.

Difficult-case writing — constructing clinical questions that probe the limits of current model reasoning.

Task length varies by stream, from roughly 45 minutes for a dialogue evaluation up to an hour or more for grading-criteria authoring. You will get a specific throughput target for whichever stream you are matched to.

AI is changing the job market in three very different ways.
In the US, China, and Russia, layoffs follow different scripts. The outcome is increasingly similar: smaller teams, more AI, and higher expectations for everyone who stays.

A few days ago, Oracle started another round of layoffs. Some employees reportedly received a 6 a.m. email telling them it was their last day 🐀

Over the past year, Oracle’s global headcount fell from 162,000 to 141,000. At the same time, the company has been investing heavily in AI data centres.

This pattern goes far beyond Oracle. Big Tech hired aggressively in the early 2020s. Payrolls grew, the market changed, and now companies need money for AI and infrastructure.

Here’s what layoffs look like across three markets:
🇺🇸 The US: Layoffs can happen overnight. Companies usually frame them as restructuring, resource reallocation, or investment in AI

🇨🇳 China: Cuts tend to be quieter. Contracts are not renewed, hiring is frozen, and several roles are merged into one. The remaining employees get AI tools—and more work

🇷🇺 Russia: AI infrastructure is less developed, so layoffs are driven mainly by falling demand and cost-cutting. AI then helps companies avoid rehiring. Ten people leave, three return, and they are expected to become AI-native

What does this mean for hiring?
Editors, designers, and marketers who still do everything manually are in a vulnerable position. Companies can already hand part of that work to AI and reduce costs.

So, which skills can help you stay competitive?
→ Business and product metrics. Understand how your work affects revenue, conversion, retention, acquisition costs, and support workload

→ Rapid hypothesis testing. Run research, build a prototype, launch a test, and make decisions based on the results

→ AI-powered workflows. Automate repetitive tasks, analyse data, create A/B test variations, and speed up production.
The market increasingly rewards people who understand the business problem, test solutions quickly, and deliver more with fewer resources.

What happened at World Space Business Week 26?

World Space Business Week wrapped in Paris last week, and told a clear story: sovereignty and defense budgets are now the industry's real growth engine, and Europe's New Space startups are finally winning the contracts to prove it.

🛰️Sovereignty is rewriting the buyer's list. 

Novaspace CEO Pacome Revillon presented forecasts showing defense space budgets climbing to $121B by 2028 (from $74B in 2025) and ISR satellite launches quadrupling this decade. ICEYE was tapped by ESA to lead a European consortium designing the EU's sovereign Earth Observation Governmental Service.

💰The money is real, the models aren't finished. 

Space-tech VC hit $11.3B in H1 2026 alone.

Open Cosmos closed a €300M Series C days before the conference, crossing into unicorn territory and explicitly earmarking the funds to scale engineering, manufacturing, and software teams across four countries. 

Eutelsat CEO Jean-François Fallacher expanded its Airbus order to 669 OneWeb satellites plus 264 for Europe's IRIS² constellation.

🤝Vertical integration is the strategy of the moment. 

Space42's Karim Michel Sabbagh put it bluntly: the industry is "moving from a world that is quite monolithic" to multi-domain, vertically integrated players. A UAE-France consortium (Loft Orbital, Marlan Space) backed that up with a $1B commitment to scale an AI-enabled EO constellation from 10 to 50 satellites.

📡Direct-to-device keeps adding partners, not answers. Viasat's Mark Dankberg, Iridium's Matt Desch, and AST SpaceMobile's Scott Wisniewski all shared the stage, but spectrum, capital risk, and network governance remain unresolved even as partnerships multiply.

What it means for talent:

Funded scale-ups are hiring hard across engineering, manufacturing, and software, but the market has a real experience cliff. Mid-career systems engineers, flight software, propulsion, and RF specialists are in short supply, and clearance requirements are stretching timelines further.

If your organization is trying to scale in sovereign space, defense ISR, or commercial EO right now, the war for senior technical talent is only getting sharper.

If you were in Paris, let me know what stood out to you.

A rushed technical hire rarely fails in week one.

It fails in month four, when nobody remembers the decision was made in a hurry.

The pressure is real. A roadmap slips, a client is waiting, a key engineer resigns. So the bar drops a little, and "good enough" becomes the standard.

The cost shows up later, and not on any hiring dashboard:

Senior engineers spend more time on reviews and rework, so their own output drops first.
Small shortcuts in design add up to tech debt someone pays for next year.

Onboarding gets rushed too, so the new hire stays unsure and the team stays cautious.

Strong people get tired of cleaning up after weak fits, and some leave.

AI adds a new twist. Coding assistants can make an average engineer look productive on routine tasks, and that speed is genuinely useful. But they don't replace judgement on architecture, trade-offs, or knowing when generated code is wrong. That judgement is harder to spot in a quick interview, which makes rushed hiring riskier, not safer.

A few things help when time is short:

-Define the problem before the job title.
-Test how people reason, not only what they have built.
-Use a short contract or contract-to-hire period when the need is urgent but unclear.
-Keep the bar where it was, even when the deadline moves.
-The teams that hire well under pressure usually did one thing early. They decided what a good hire looks like before the pressure started.

What is the most expensive hiring shortcut you have seen?

You only have to search LinkedIn, job boards, anywhere, and type in "AI" or "Artificial Intelligence" to see an abundance of roles being advertised right now. It's not surprising given the UK's AI sector alone now comprises over 5,800 businesses generating roughly £24 billion a year. Everyone wants to be involved with, or using, AI in some capacity, and that can be considered both a blessing and a curse.

From a client perspective, more candidates wanting to align their focus into AI means more people applying for every AI role posted, which means more work for internal talent teams sifting through it all. Recent research shows "AI user" roles, people applying AI within an existing job function, are growing nearly three times faster than genuine AI "developer"/specialist roles (65.8% vs 21.6% YoY). The impact? It means a lot of that application volume is candidates repositioning toward AI language rather than people who can actually build and ship it, and the very best of the best are often not the ones actively applying at all. This means the real question isn't how many CVs came in; it's whether you're actually reaching the top talent, or just the most active job seekers.

From a candidate perspective, more jobs on the surface looks great, but what a company says it's doing with AI and the reality on the ground are often two very different things. ONS figures show AI adoption among UK businesses has nearly tripled since 2023, from around 12% to 35%; but among the businesses that have adopted it, the average one is only using 1.6 AI technologies, and just 11% have trained more than half their workforce on it. The headline number is growing fast; the depth behind it isn't keeping pace. A business can have all the right intentions, but if the foundations, data, skills, structure, aren't in place yet, no amount of ambition alone gets you to a successful outcome, or a role that lives up to what was advertised.

This is where a genuine AI focused talent partner like Cubiq adds value on both sides.

If you're a client looking for talent, we have real, deep roots into the talent pool; we know the top talent, their move motivators and where their expertise lies; that means we can ensure the best-fit contract or permanent candidates are put forward for your needs.

If you're looking for a new role in AI, we have consultants within their own niches with deep specialist knowledge who know what businesses in that space are actually doing, where they are on their journey, and can align your own aspirations with the right environment.

If you sit on either side of that fence, searching for a role or hiring for one, and think a conversation would help, I'm always happy to find time to talk, so please feel free to reach out.

🚢 The world's best-performing ETF this year has nothing to do with AI, crypto, or tech stocks. It's about the cost of moving oil across the ocean.
$BWET (Breakwave Tanker Shipping ETF) is up +5,820% over the last 12 months and +4,556% year-to-date in 2026 — making it the top-performing ETF in the world.
What is $BWET actually tracking?
It holds crude oil tanker freight futures — contracts tied to the cost of hiring supertankers (VLCCs) to move crude from the Middle East to China, and from West Africa to Europe. It doesn't hold oil, ships, or energy stocks. It's a pure bet on shipping cost.
Why has it exploded?
⚔️ The US-Iran war (since Feb 2026) has severely disrupted traffic through the Strait of Hormuz — a chokepoint that once saw ~125 vessels cross daily, now down to a handful.
🛢️ Tanker owners are demanding enormous risk premiums to sail Gulf waters, pushing freight rates from ~$75,000-100,000/day to several hundred thousand dollars/day.
🌍 Compounding disruptions — Houthi activity near the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, Russia's Black Sea shipping issues, and a Russian diesel export ban — have tightened global fuel and shipping capacity simultaneously.
What this means for supply chains, logistics & the world economy:
📦 Freight costs are a hidden tax on everything shipped by sea — energy, food, manufactured goods.
⛽ Diesel and crude transport costs are already spilling into record-high diesel prices at the pump, squeezing farmers, truckers and consumers alike.
📈 Inflationary pressure is building globally, not just at gas stations — insurance, rerouting, and longer voyages all add cost and time to global trade.
🌐 It's a stark reminder of how fragile and interconnected global logistics really are — a single geopolitical flashpoint can ripple through energy markets, freight, agriculture, and household budgets worldwide.
We are in the middle of an unprecedented global energy and shipping shock — and the markets are pricing it in real time.
